pieces.name: Boot CPU hand-back
pieces.known: `SYSTEM_SUSPEND` returns through the kernel’s `cpu_resume`, 20 of 20 on all CPUs (image 48). It works with retention through `deep_wfi()`; an inline `dsb sy; isb; wfi` never woke (images 37 to 40). Powered down without retention, the core never re-enters at RVBAR (images 32 to 36).
pieces.next: A real S2R wake comes back through RVBAR; image 51 resumes the kernel from there, not reached yet

pieces.name: Wake sources
pieces.known: Deep WFI with AIC lines 724 (alarm) and 865 (SMC mailbox) unmasked. The power key wakes on 865.
pieces.next: Lid; stop the SMC’s early `Elec Cause` syslog wakes

pieces.name: AIC
pieces.known: Save and mask every bank, restore on resume (syscore). It runs on every Phase 2 cycle. Because it masks everything, wake detection has to come from the PMU/SMC side.

pieces.name: SMC handshake
pieces.known: `slpw`, `slpa` and `waka` in the macOS order, with `WKTP`, `pmVC` and AP power IDLE/ON. After a real S2R wake the SMC answers keys and events. It stays in its sleep power state (`MEPS` 1) after `waka`, which is what keeps the Wi-Fi and SD rails off.

pieces.name: PMP
pieces.known: IDLE works in s2idle (acks in about 400 us) and now after `slpa` too (run C again, 2026-11-05 21:22: accepted, no crash; the 16:01 crash was the test kernel’s double `SetAPPower`). The wake from IDLE fails without a power cycle (-62). The display requests are released for sleep in normal suspends; once the PMP is IDLE the release is refused (`-EALREADY`), so it has to move before `slpa`. A PMGR reset of `ps_pmp` crashes the SoC. Since 2026-11-06 the test kernel can withdraw every request (the displays and ISP_SYS) just before `slpa`, while the PMP still acks (`deep_steps` 32, run Q: 0xf000 to 0, back after the wake); in C, I, J and L the noirq release came after the IDLE and was refused.

pieces.name: AOP
pieces.known: The macOS handshake (queues stopped, `SetAPPower` 0x201) before the sleep, `SetAPPower` ON and the queues started again from syscore resume, before the secondaries come back; works in every real S2R wake.

pieces.name: Secondary CPUs
pieces.known: CPU_OFF parks the core in Aura’s retention deep WFI loop; CPU_ON hands it back through the spin table, with `CYC_OVRD` restored first. 20 of 20 suspend cycles with all nine.
pieces.next: Runtime hotplug outside suspend; RVBAR re-entry after real power loss

pieces.name: PMGR quiesce, S2R timer
pieces.known: Aura's commit puts the SoC into SLP_S2R (the PMGR counter counts it) and the RTC alarm wakes it through RVBAR, every run since R57AL. The long hunt (the 75-86 s resets, runs D to R22B) ended once the remaining entry state was in place.

findings.title: A night on battery: 0.375 W, 99.6% of it in S2R
findings.body: With the lid closed on the real Omarchy desktop, the Mac spent 7.14 h asleep and was in S2R for 99.6% of that time, using 2.679 Wh (5% of the battery, 70% to 65%): 0.375 W on average. The old s2idle figure on this Mac was about 1.48 W; macOS about 0.24 W. One night, one run. A GPU client drawing across 10 sleeps also came back every time, the case another tester had reported as hanging on the second sleep.

findings.title: S2R is now the default boot, with working speakers
findings.body: Aura 129 passes the Mac's real amplifier levels, the speaker driver unlocks with speaker protection running, and the owner heard a quiet tone before and after a suspend. Aura 129 is now the permanent `boot.bin` and a plain reboot (no test flag) lands in the S2R kernel. The stock images stay on the ESP for recovery.

findings.title: Real S2R from the live Omarchy desktop works (7.3.0-s2r73+, Aura 128)
findings.body: A real `systemctl suspend` in Hyprland slept 997.8 s (16 min 38 s) in SLP_S2R and woke with Hyprland, GPU rendering, display and backlight, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, SD, NVMe, USB, PMP and SEP all working and no errors. Every device now returns with zero userspace unbinds. Aura 129 (real amp levels from the Mac's device tree, so the speakers can be enabled safely) is booted and reports 'Speaker volumes unlocked'; the playback check before and after a suspend is next.

findings.title: The PCIe shutdown isn't needed; one change was the whole fix (R61R)
findings.body: A third run, this time without the orderly PCIe shutdown before the sleep. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the SD reader came back again and Wi-Fi rejoined the network: 3 of 3. So the fix is one change in our sleep entry: Aura leaves the PCIe power domains on at the commit. The existing relink after the wake does the rest.

findings.title: Wi-Fi joins the network after a real S2R, 2 of 2 (R61Q)
findings.body: A repeat of R61P with a Wi-Fi check after the wake. Both links trained on the first relink again. Wi-Fi scanned 51 networks and joined the home network on its own, about 20 s after the wake. Bluetooth and the SD controller came up as well.

findings.title: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the SD reader come back after a real S2R (R61P)
findings.body: The cause was our own sleep entry. Since image 64, Aura powered off the three PCIe power domains (apcie_gp_sys, apcie_gpshr_sys, apcie_gp) at the commit, because macOS has them off at that point. With that step left out (aura-ctl bit 20), the sleep still commits (PMU 0x601f = aa, NVMe cold-starts) and both links train on the first relink after the wake. The BCM4388 loads its firmware, Bluetooth comes up as hci0, and the SD controller is found again. The SMC's MEPS 1 after waka is normal: macOS shows it too.

findings.title: macOS's PCIe shutdown before the sleep doesn't bring Wi-Fi back (R61O)
findings.body: Before the sleep, Linux now powers down the Wi-Fi and SD reader links in an orderly way, as macOS does: the devices go to their low-power state, the links into L2, reset held and clock off. All of it ran cleanly, but after the wake the links still never find a device. The PCIe side now matches a machine where Wi-Fi does come back, so the missing piece is the power to the devices, which the SMC still holds off.

findings.title: Holding the radio in reset through the sleep changes nothing (R61N)
findings.body: The newer Apple sleep drivers hold the Wi-Fi chip in reset during the sleep and release it after. Our wake already resets and re-powers the slot before every relink attempt, and the links still never train. Wi-Fi and the SD reader stay blocked on the SMC's sleep power state; we are waiting on answers from people whose machines get their radios back.

findings.title: SMC stays in its sleep state even with the display back (R61M7)
findings.body: With the display coprocessor restored, the SMC still reports its sleep power state after the wake, and Wi-Fi and SD stay off. The SMC's state machine can't be moved from the AP, and iBoot (which might do it on a cold boot) is encrypted. Wi-Fi/SD after S2R is blocked.

findings.title: Internal display comes back after a real S2R (R61M6)
findings.body: After the wake the display coprocessor is cold-started from clean firmware data, and Linux plays iBoot's part (panel power-on, set mode) before the normal start. The display driver then starts fully: panel detected, 6 modes, panel rail back at 1.29 V, no crash. Wi-Fi and SD still do not come back; the display was not what blocks them.

findings.title: Internal display's iBoot service answers after the wake (R61M5)
findings.body: After the cold restart, Linux can now talk to the internal display coprocessor's iBoot service. The panel reported as unplugged because it was not yet powered. R61M6 powers it on first, then sets the mode.

findings.title: DCP firmware wants iBoot's display session first (R61M4)
findings.body: Reading the DCP firmware shows the display driver start checks a flag that only iBoot's display session sets. A copy of the firmware data taken at boot does not restart. R61M5 has Linux play iBoot's part (power on, set mode) before the normal start.

findings.title: DCP firmware cold-boots after the wake (R61M3)
findings.body: With a clean data segment plus iBoot's boot arguments, the display coprocessor's firmware restarts cleanly after a real S2R and all its services start. The display driver then refuses because iBoot did not bring the panel up this time. R61M4 restores the state iBoot hands over instead.

findings.title: DCP restart: assert gone with pristine data (R61M2)
findings.body: Restoring the DCP firmware's data segment from macOS's file stops the crash after the wake, but the firmware then stays silent. It has lost the boot arguments iBoot writes into a tagged block (bArg and others). R61M3 keeps that block.

findings.title: DCP firmware addresses confirmed (R61M)
findings.body: After the wake, the firmware code in memory matches macOS's DCP file except for 2 words, so the addresses are right. A check that was too strict left the data segment unrestored, so the restart crashed as before. R61M2 restores it.

findings.title: DCP firmware data segment located (R61L)
findings.body: The live ADT gives the DCP firmware's segments: __TEXT at 0x10000230000 (6 MB) and __DATA at 0x107d2c94000 (3 MB). They match macOS's DCP.img4 exactly, so the restart after the wake can begin from a pristine __DATA. R61M tests that.

findings.title: The display firmware needs a clean copy of its memory to restart
findings.body: Given back its old memory, the display firmware gets further but then trips over its own leftover state from before the sleep. macOS has a way to put the firmware's memory back to a clean copy before restarting it. The next test reads the boot loader's description of that memory, so we can save a clean copy at boot and restore it after the wake.

findings.title: The display firmware crashes when its services are set up a second time
findings.body: The display firmware survives the restart itself, but crashes as soon as the driver sets up its services again with new memory, because the firmware still remembers the old setup. The next test gives it back exactly the memory it had before the sleep, one service at a time.

findings.title: The display firmware now restarts cleanly after the wake
findings.body: Keeping the display firmware's buffers as they were across the sleep (the same trick as for the storage controller) lets it restart after a real sleep without crashing. The display itself is not back yet: the next test starts the display service and turns the panel on.

findings.title: The display firmware starts again after the wake, then crashes
findings.body: For the first time, the display coprocessor's firmware started again after a real sleep: its boot address survives the power cut, and it completed its startup handshake. A few milliseconds later it crashed in its shared-memory code, most likely because it restarts on top of the memory it had before the sleep. The next test keeps its buffers as they were, which is what made the same restart work for the storage controller.

findings.title: First real restart of the display firmware after the wake
findings.body: A full read of every PCIe controller and PHY register found nothing the wake path misses on the controller side. The one setting that still differs from macOS after its wake comes back on another tester's machine when the display firmware is restarted, and the display needs that restart anyway. The test kernel now cold-starts the display firmware after the wake; the next test checks whether the screen's power and the Wi-Fi/SD slots come back with it.

findings.title: Resetting the PCIe controller on the wake path did not bring the slots back
findings.body: A new boot-loader build powers the PCIe controller fully off on the wake path and sets it up again from scratch. That worked mechanically, but the Wi-Fi and SD links still do not come up. The next test reads every PCIe controller and PHY register before and after the sleep, not just the ones macOS sets, to find what is left over.

findings.title: The sleep never resets the PCIe controller
findings.body: The power-state dump shows the PCIe controller is only clock-gated during the sleep, never powered off, so it keeps leftover state that a cold boot never has. Restarting the display driver after the wake did not help. The next test powers the PCIe controller fully off on the wake path before setting it up again, as a cold boot does.

findings.title: Every PCIe power domain comes back after the wake
findings.body: All 374 PMGR power-state registers macOS programs were read before the sleep and after the wake. The PCIe domains are all fully on after the wake; only the 'was gated' flags differ. So the Wi-Fi/SD slots are not missing a power domain. Next: restart the display firmware after the wake, since a running display firmware may be what restores a PMU setting macOS has after its wake and we do not.

findings.title: Our test kernel stops the display firmware for every sleep and never restarts it
findings.body: A test switch added early on shuts the display coprocessor's firmware down before each deep sleep and leaves it off after the wake. Another tester found on his machine that the missing power rail comes back only when that firmware is restarted. The next test sleeps with the firmware left running.

findings.title: A runtime power cut can be recovered; a sleep cannot (yet)
findings.body: After cutting the Wi-Fi and SD power on a running system, our PCIe relink brings both devices back. After a real sleep the same relink finds no device at all, so the sleep turns off something more, most likely a supply rail. The next test checks whether that rail depends on the display coprocessor, as another tester found on a similar Mac.

findings.title: The Wi-Fi/SD failure reproduces without a sleep
findings.body: Switching the Wi-Fi radio's power (REG_ON) or the SD reader's power off and on again on a running system leaves both links in Detect and the devices unreadable, exactly as after a wake. So the fault is in how the slots are brought back after any power loss, and it can now be tested in 2-minute boots instead of full sleep cycles.

findings.title: macOS 13.5 boots fully under our hypervisor with PCIe on
findings.body: For the first time macOS ran to its lock screen under the m1n1-based hypervisor with the Wi-Fi and SD slots enabled (14.8.9 hung during boot). At boot it powers the two slots with the same two SMC writes Linux uses (SD power gP16 and Wi-Fi REG_ON gP0d), so nothing is missing at boot. Next: trace a macOS sleep and wake with the PMU and PCIe traced.

findings.title: R60M: Wi-Fi, BT and SD are gone after the wake even with their drivers unbound
findings.body: With brcmfmac, hci_bcm4377 and sdhci-pci unbound before the sleep, all three devices still read ffffffff after the wake and the links stay in Detect. So it is not the drivers' suspend path. nekolyanich's M2 Max answers after its wake; the remaining lead is the VR3l rail (1.29 V before, 0.005 V after), which on his machine comes back with a display-coprocessor restart. Next: the macOS 13.5 trace.

findings.title: R60L: the SMC's VDD_CIO switch (pmVC) is not what keeps Wi-Fi and SD down
findings.body: After the wake, six pmVC values (0x1ff, 0x1fff, 0x10f, 0x180, 0x0, 0x101) were written and the PCIe links retried after each. Every write was accepted, but both links stayed in Detect and the SMC's power state (MEPS 000102010004) never changed. Next lead: trace macOS 13.5 bringing the slots up under the m1n1 hypervisor, as DJ suggests.

findings.title: R60K: Andreas Fernandez's apcie quiesce handshake makes no difference
findings.body: Aura image 125 does the PCIe handshake from his M1 Pro sleep code (macOS quiesceHW step 24b) at our guessed M2 Pro address, 0x59c008014 / 0x59c0082bc, and puts it back at the wake. It ran (crumbs 07), the wake worked, but Wi-Fi and the SD reader still stay in Detect and the SMC still reports MEPS 000102010004. Both words read 0 before the sleep, so the M2 Pro offsets may differ.

findings.title: R60J: the wake works without the 0x50 boot stage; Wi-Fi power still off
findings.body: Skipping the PMU boot stage that macOS 13.5 sets for sleep makes no difference: the Mac sleeps and wakes the same, and the SMC still stays in its sleep power state. A PMU comparison within one boot confirms which power-enable bits stay off after the wake.

findings.title: R60I: the PCIe controller comes back exactly; Wi-Fi's power doesn't
findings.body: Every PCIe controller, port and PHY register reads the same before the sleep and after the wake, so the controller side is fully restored. The Wi-Fi module and SD reader stay unpowered because the SMC and PMU stay in a sleep power state after the wake, which we can't change from Linux. We've asked nekolyanich and Andreas Fernandez what their machines show.

findings.title: R60H: SD reader power cut across the sleep, no change
findings.body: The SD power was switched off before the sleep and back on at the wake as planned, and the SMC sequence now matches Andreas Fernandez's M1 Pro one. Wi-Fi and the SD reader still don't show up on PCIe. Since both fail the same way, R60I compares the PCIe controller's registers before the sleep and after the wake.

findings.title: R60H armed: SD reader power off across the sleep (Andreas Fernandez's t600x recipe)
findings.body: Andreas's M1 Pro S2R, where Wi-Fi comes back, switches the SD reader's power (SMC GPIO) off just before the final sleep command and on again first thing at the wake, and sets pmVC = 0x100. We never did either. R60H does both on the M2 Pro (gP16).

findings.title: R60G: pmVC around the sleep changes nothing; the rail readings were not the cause
findings.body: pmVC (macOS's toggle_vdd_cio) was accepted before slpa and after waka, but the SMC still stays in power state 1 and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the SD reader stay absent. The supply readings that looked like dropped rails move with load (one read 0 V before the sleep and 1.29 V after the wake), so that explanation is withdrawn.

findings.title: R60G prepared: pmVC around slpa and after waka (lead from upstream T6050 sleep)
findings.body: Upstream Aurora's T6050 deep sleep, which brings Wi-Fi and the SD reader back, sends SMC key pmVC (macOS PMGR's toggle_vdd_cio, 0x100 | CIO requesters) 35 ms before slpa and 58 ms after waka. We never write it (reads 0 on the J414s), and our SMC stays in MEPS 1 with rails off after waka. Test R60G built (UKI pmp18, s2r_pmvc=0x107), not armed while the owner uses the laptop. Upstream i2c-pasemi runtime PM now covers our i2c fix.

findings.title: R60E-R60F: the SMC message to sleep is required, and the boot-time message does not bring it back
findings.body: Without the sleep message the system controller is unusable after the wake; with it, it stays in its sleep power state, and the boot-time message macOS sends is refused. Waiting on the M2 Pro developer we work with for how their wake gets the controller back to awake.

findings.title: R60D: after the wake the system controller stays in its sleep power state
findings.body: A dump of every SMC key before and after the sleep shows its power-state record going from 4 to 1 and staying there after the wake message, with a few supply rails still off. That would explain the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module and the SD reader both being gone. Asked the M2 Pro developer we work with how their wake moves the SMC back.

findings.title: R60A: first full log from after a wake: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the SD reader are all gone
findings.body: With the post-wake log written to /boot, the full kernel log shows all three PCIe devices (Wi-Fi, its Bluetooth function, the SD card reader) unreachable after the wake. A before/after dump of the power-management chip shows a few settings the sleep changed and nothing restores. R60B puts them back.

findings.title: R59Y: the PCIe port never sees the Wi-Fi chip
findings.body: After the wake the port's link state machine stays in receiver detection: electrically, the Wi-Fi chip is not on the link. R59Z checks the port's own PHY against a normal boot and tries a full one-second power cycle of the chip.

findings.title: R59X: the Wi-Fi radio stays powered through the sleep
findings.body: The radio's power/enable line (REG_ON) reads high before, during and after the sleep, and its reset and clock-request pins match a normal boot. Yet the PCIe link to the Wi-Fi chip never comes up. R59Y reads the link state machine to see how far it gets.

findings.title: R59V-R59W: the Wi-Fi slot is powered and out of reset after the wake, but never links
findings.body: Slot power and the reset line both read correct after the wake, and the PCIe port is ready, yet the Wi-Fi chip is never detected. Next lead: the clock-request pin mux, which Linux does not put back after the power cut.

findings.title: R59U: USB works after a real S2R power cut
findings.body: With three fixes (I2C controller re-init, Type-C PHY restore, and the M2 Pro dummy-PHY bit) every health check passes after the wake: NVMe, USB, keyboard, battery/SMC, RTC and SEP. Wi-Fi is the last device missing.

findings.title: R59T: the Type-C PHY loses a bit iBoot set, which the driver never sets on M2 Pro
findings.body: The PHY handshake only works while a dummy-PHY enable bit is set. iBoot sets it, a power cut clears it, and the driver only restores it on M3-class chips. One port on main already has it cleared without any sleep, so this is a general bug. R59U tests the fix: treat the M2 Pro like M3 here.

findings.title: R59S: USB now stops at the Type-C PHY handshake
findings.body: With the I2C fix the next failure after the wake is the PHY waiting for the USB controller to acknowledge a handshake. R59T records the registers at that moment to see whether the controller is still held in reset or lost its clock.

findings.title: R59R: the Type-C controllers answer again after the wake
findings.body: Re-initialising the Apple I2C controller on resume removed the PD-controller errors. USB is still down: the next error is in the Type-C PHY, being narrowed down in R59S.

findings.title: R59Q: USB after the wake fails at the PD controllers' I2C bus
findings.body: The first USB error after the wake is the Type-C PD controller timing out on I2C (-ETIME). The Apple I2C driver has no resume callback, so after the power cut its controller is never set up again. R59R tests a fix that re-initialises it on resume.

findings.title: R59P: a 5-minute sleep comes back too
findings.body: A 5-minute S2R sleep resumes like the 30 s ones: userspace, PMP restart and NVMe all back, clean reboot, nothing fired during the cut. USB and Wi-Fi still missing after the wake.

findings.title: R59L: the NVMe disk comes back after a real S2R power cut
findings.body: With the power-manager coprocessor (PMP) restarted after the cut and the storage controller (ANS) handled the way Andreas Fernandez does on M1 Pro (idled with its state and buffers kept instead of shut down, its SART power word and ADT tunables restored, a longer power-on wait), the ANS boots again after the wake: NVMe is live and reads work. Keyboard, SMC, RTC and SEP work as well, with no kernel warnings. Still open: USB and Wi-Fi (the PCIe rescan currently trips a kernel BUG and is switched off).

findings.title: R59E: the power-manager coprocessor (PMP) now comes back after the wake
findings.body: Ported Andreas Fernandez's M1 Pro method to the M2 Pro: before the sleep the PMP is idled and stopped and its SRAM firmware image saved; after the wake the SRAM, its DMA filters and DART are put back and the firmware is booted again. First try: the PMP said hello again after a real power cut, and resume stayed 16 of 16. The storage controller still fails to power up; next its own restore (SART power word, longer wait, tunables).

findings.title: R58P-R58U: resume works 6 of 6; first device picture after the wake
findings.body: Since the gpio-domain fix every test sleeps, wakes on the alarm, returns to userspace and reboots cleanly (6 of 6). A health check after the wake: keyboard, battery/SMC, RTC and SEP work, with no kernel warnings or timeouts. Not yet: NVMe (the disk, needed for the real install), some USB devices, and Wi-Fi (the PCIe port is set up again but the link does not train).

findings.title: R58C-R58P: this morning's no-sleep regression found and fixed (gpio power domain)
findings.body: From about 07:50 no test slept, even with last night's exact setup. Entry crumbs in Aura (image 122) showed Linux does call SYSTEM_SUSPEND, and Aura then hangs reading the pinctrl block for its GPIO snapshot: genpd had switched that block's power domain (gpio) off during suspend. Keeping the gpio domain on (R58P) restored the full cycle: real sleep, alarm wake, Linux back to userspace, clean reboot. The proper fix is to keep that domain on through sleep, as macOS does. Two side issues cost runs: the ntfy.sh daily cap (test boots now also log to a LAN sink) and kernel crumbs that hang once the AIC is masked.

findings.title: R57AM-R57AR: the resume reproduces 6 of 6; Wi-Fi does not come back
findings.body: Every run since R57AL resumes to userspace. After the wake the Wi-Fi's PCIe link stays down (in L2), its power enable (SMC gpio 13) reads low, and the port is not running, even after Aura restores the per-port MSI setup and the AP GPIO block and a test module replays the slot power-up. The fix belongs in the PCIe driver's resume (nekolyanich: redo probe's per-port setup), which needs a patched kernel.

findings.title: R57AL: Linux resumes to userspace after a real S2R sleep
findings.body: First full round trip on this Mac: a real 27 s S2R sleep, alarm wake, the kernel resume completes, and echo mem returns 0 with all 10 CPUs online (PMU stamps from the job). Two fixes in Aura's wake path, before Linux resumes, got it there: rerunning the internal PCIe (apcie) bring-up (nekolyanich's fix) and restoring the SEP power domain, which the cut leaves with DEV_DISABLE set. Wi-Fi does not come back yet, so the job could not report over the network.

findings.title: R57AI: the first fault is a PCIe DART read in apple_dart_resume
findings.body: The stack under the SError: a synchronous abort in apple_dart_resume (its first register read), with the fault at physical 0x595000000, the DART of PCIe port 1 (the SD reader). The real power cut wipes the internal PCIe setup, as nekolyanich found, and they rerun m1n1's apcie bring-up at the wake. Image 116 does that in Aura's wake path before Linux resumes.

findings.title: R57AF: the woken kernel dies of an SError
findings.body: A stack record of the panic, taken by Aura on the reset (kernel panic, EFI ResetSystem, U-Boot, Aura's PSCI handler walking the kernel's frame records into the PMU's 40-byte scratch), names arm64_serror_panic. So within a second of the real S2R wake the kernel touches hardware that answers with an external abort, most likely a block that is still unpowered or unclocked. The next run records the frames below it (the interrupted code) and ESR.

findings.title: R57X-R57AD: the panic is reproducible, and the capture path reaches Aura
findings.body: Five more sleeps: each time a real 28 s sleep, an alarm wake, and a panic (reset at alarm + kernel.panic). The panic's restart reaches Aura's PSCI handler via EFI ResetSystem in U-Boot (proved by a 5 s watchdog in the handler: reset at alarm + 32 s). macsmc-reboot's SMC restart wins over PSCI, and U-Boot did not advertise ResetSystem, which needed fixing first. The PMU write from that context still fails; image 111 is finding out why.

findings.title: R57W: the woken kernel panics within about a second of the wake
findings.body: With kernel.panic set to 27 s the PMU reset stamp moved to the alarm + 27 s (it was + 10 s with panic=10). So Linux does run after the real S2R wake and panics almost at once. Panic-on-oops is off, so it is a real panic (an SError, or an oops in interrupt or idle context). Aura image 106 records the panicking stack in PMU scratch during the kernel's PSCI SYSTEM_RESET, to name the function.

findings.title: R57V2: a +120 s sleep lasts 118 s, and the reset comes about 10 s after the alarm wake
findings.body: With the alarm at +120 s the PMU scratch shows a 118 s real sleep. The PMU reset stamp (0x1419) is 10 s after the RTC alarm (0x140c), so the reset follows the wake, not the commit (nekolyanich read WD2 as disarmed after a real wake). 10 s matches panic=10 on the test kernel and Aura's 10 s stage-1 RVBAR watchdog; R57W (panic=27) tells them apart. Both a panic and a hang point to the first second of the kernel's resume.

findings.title: R57O-R57U: any patched test kernel fails to boot the test
findings.body: Nine test boots with a patched kernel (a PMU-scratch crumb in the device PM path, then the crumb code in its own file, then an empty crumb body, with the test root's modules and the initramfs rebuilt to match) all came back after 78-79 s with no reports. The unpatched rebuild boots (R57P, 92 s with reports). Only an identical rebuild boots, so the test boot depends on something about the exact Image that we cannot see without a console. Kernel-side crumbs are blocked until we can see why.

findings.title: R57N: DRAM does not survive the reset
findings.body: A persistent trace buffer on a reserved RAM page had a valid header at test boot and read back as all zeros from main after the sleep and reset. RAM logs (ramoops, pstore console, persistent trace) cannot show where resume stops on this setup; only the PMU scratch bytes survive.

findings.title: Old toolchain reproduces the working test kernel
findings.body: Kernels built with clang 23.1.5 / rustc 1.100 (or GCC) did not boot the test; the same config rebuilt with clang 23.1.4 / rustc 1.99.1 (extracted from the pacman cache) does (R57L4, R57P). Config-changed kernels (pstore console, DPM watchdog) also fail the test boot, which the later patched-kernel runs show is not about the config alone.

findings.title: R57L2b: the rebuilt kernel did not boot the test
findings.body: The clang-built kernel with the pstore console came back after 79 s with no reports and an empty RAM page, so it never ran the test, like the GCC build. The only differences from the working Nov 9 kernel are the compiler versions (clang 23.1.5, rustc 1.100) and the console option. A control build with the console off is running to tell which one it is.

findings.title: R57L control: the RAM log tests could not have worked
findings.body: The control run (markers then a normal reboot) and a live check on main both showed an empty reserved page, because the test kernel is built without the pstore console option, so ramoops only keeps panic dumps and never logs ordinary messages. Next: build the same kernel with that option on and repeat.

findings.title: R57K2: the reserved RAM page stays untouched, and holds no console log
findings.body: With main now reserving the page too, it read back all zeros after the sleep, wake and reset: the sleep and wake happened again (22 s), but no console text or panic record was there. So either DRAM is cleared by the reset, or nothing was written. Next: a control run that only logs a marker and reboots normally.

findings.title: R57K: the crash-log page is reused by the next boot before it can be read
findings.body: With only reserve_mem in the kernel line the sleep and RTC wake happen again (23 s), and the Mac resets about 59 s after the commit. The reserved RAM page held ordinary kernel data when read on the main system, so the main boot had already reused it. A RAM log needs the main kernel to reserve the same page, or the crumbs have to go somewhere that survives, such as the power chip's scratch bytes.

findings.title: R57A3: the plain recipe still wakes for real (23 s sleep) and then stalls
findings.body: Plain test boot with only aop.sleep_ap_idle=3: the PMU scratch shows the Aura return (0x22) and a 23 s sleep, and the Mac resets 59 s after the commit. The run with reserve_mem plus the ramoops module and panic options (R57J3) left no wake stamp at all, so those additions may change the sleep. Next: keep the console log in the reserved RAM (R57K) to see how far Linux got.

findings.title: R57J3: the commit ran, no wake and no panic record
findings.body: The test boot reached the commit (16:15:46) and the Mac reset 59 s later, the same time as the no-wake reset in nekolyanich's notes. The PMU scratch was not rewritten (so no wake stamp was left) and the reserved RAM page for the panic log read all zeros. Either the SoC reset wipes or the firmware scrubs that page, or the kernel never panicked. Next: a kernel crumb written straight to PMU scratch, and checking whether the alarm armed.

findings.title: R57D: unbinding display, DCPs, PCIe, SIO and NVMe does not help
findings.body: With those five devices unbound before the sleep the result is the same (real 24 s sleep, alarm wake, no userspace; boot_stage stays 0x50 this time). The hang or panic after the wake is not in those drivers. Because the reset comes about 25 s after the wake, with panic=10 it is probably a panic right after the wake; next step is ramoops to read it.

findings.title: R57E-R57K void: the test boot used the wrong kernel
findings.body: These runs used a kernel build whose drivers were not in the test root, so the power chip, clock and Wi-Fi never loaded, the sleep never ran and the readings were stale. Ignore them; R57J redoes the capture another way. Original text: A ramoops region above the kernel memory limit was read from the main system after the failed wake and holds only zeros, so there is no panic text. Either DRAM there does not survive the reset or ramoops did not load. R57F writes a known pattern there before the sleep to find out which.

findings.title: R57C: the stall after the wake is not the secondary CPUs
findings.body: With every secondary offlined before the sleep (so the kernel neither stops nor re-enables any), the result is the same as R57A: real sleep (SLP_S2R 22 s for a +25 s alarm), alarm wake, boot_stage 0x30 (resume_early ran), but echo mem never returns and the kernel is reset. So the hang is in the device resume, not the CPU bring-up.

findings.title: macOS 14.8.9 under our hypervisor does not sleep either (R53c)
findings.body: With cluster_power=0, wdt=-1, clpc=0, apcie off and no tracers, the guest runs its full sleep entry (CPUSTART stop requests for CPUs 1-6 and 8-10, then the PMGR write at 0x2902801c0) and the SoC resets 60 s later, with no wake. Same as the earlier hypervisor runs, so the stall is not our Linux entry alone; it is shared with macOS under this hypervisor on this chip.

findings.title: The AOP's queues must run before the CPUs come back
findings.body: With the AOP's endpoint queues stopped across the CPU bring-up, every secondary hung in the kernel's secondary entry after Aura handed it the entry (5 runs); restarting them from syscore resume, before the secondaries, fixed it (3 runs, 12 cycles).

findings.title: The gap is SoC sleep itself
findings.body: Awake idle matches macOS once the PMP runs (5.38 W against 5.57 W, SoC 1.22 W on both). The lid-closed gap is not the devices.

findings.title: s2idle’s 1.4 W is power left on, not wakes
findings.body: The 3.2 wakes a second come from the AOP’s ambient-light and lid-angle reports and cost milliwatts. The PMP doesn’t change the drain.

findings.title: macOS tells the PMP when the system sleeps
findings.body: Read from the macOS 13.5 kernelcache: the full order of sleep and quiesce actions, the SMC `MBSE` handshake, PMGR’s last write, and the PMP’s RTKit IDLE (0x201), which is Linux’s unused `apple_rtkit_idle()`.

findings.title: `slpa` takes the storage away
findings.body: After `slpa` every NVMe access fails: in s2idle (10-22) and in five real suspends (11-04 and 05), where the Mac resumed on the alarm and the storage controller never booted again. A reboot from Linux (the dead-man switch’s) brings it back. On its own `slpa` does not put the SoC to sleep, so it cannot be the last step by itself.

findings.title: The PMP’s wake from IDLE is a power cycle
findings.body: RUN alone woke it 0 of 3. Gating its SRAM did not restart it, and resetting `ps_pmp` crashed the SoC. `ps_pmp` is pinned on by iBoot.

findings.title: ISR_EL1 is blind at EL2 under VHE
findings.body: With IMO/FMO set, Aura saw only the virtual pending state. The fix was to watch the AIC’s HW_STATE for the alarm line.

findings.title: The kernel masks the whole AIC for suspend
findings.body: `aic_syscore_suspend` masks every line, as macOS does. In real S2R the wake must be detected from the PMU/SMC side.

findings.title: A core powered down without retention doesn’t come back on an IRQ
findings.body: Across images 32 to 36 the boot core never re-entered at RVBAR. Secondaries only return through a PMGR CPU-start written by another core.

findings.title: NVMe drops cached writes on a hard reset
findings.body: The ANS firmware caches until a clean `saveCtx` shutdown. That explained the lost logs and the filesystem damage after hotplug hangs.

findings.title: The PMU RTC alarm is the timed wake
findings.body: Linux had no driver for the alarm macOS uses for dark wakes. `rtcwake -m freeze -s 30` woke after about 31 s, 3 of 3.

findings.title: Parked cores need retention, and must not keep WFI_MODE 3
findings.body: The October hotplug deaths came from two things: the CPU_OFF park powered cores down without retention, and a re-onlined core inherited `CYC_OVRD` WFI_MODE 3 from the park. With both fixed, all nine secondaries go off and come back every suspend cycle.

findings.title: A CPU_OFF that never returns leaks a preempt count
findings.body: The kernel’s EFI call path disables preemption around the firmware call. A successful CPU_OFF never comes back, so the re-onlined core started with one count too many (“scheduling while atomic”, once per core per cycle). Fixed in the test kernel.

findings.title: `slpa` alone does not put the SoC to sleep
findings.body: With every CPU in Aura and the boot core in deep WFI, `slpa` still left the SoC running. On the wake `waka` is acked, but the storage controller never acks its power-on (`IOP power acknowledgment failed: -62`). macOS does more between `slpa` and the power-down: `SetAPPower` and `SetIOPPower` to the PMP, the CPU stops and the PCPM clears.

findings.title: A live kernel with no disk is not a hang
findings.body: After the `slpa` run the watchdogs saw a healthy kernel, so nothing reset the Mac for about 15 min. Unattended `slpa` runs need a dead-man switch tied to the disk.

findings.title: The watchdog cannot cover a long sleep by itself
findings.body: WD1 counts 32 bits at 24 MHz, about 178 s at most. Aura now wakes on the EL2 physical timer every 60 s, re-arms the dog and sleeps again, so suspends of any length keep the safety net.

findings.title: Parking the CPUs alone saves almost nothing
findings.body: Suspend to RAM with every CPU in Aura’s deep WFI drew 1.365 W over 30 min on battery, and `s2idle` 1.390 and 1.413 W in the same boot. The gap to macOS’s 0.24 W is the SoC and DRAM staying up, which only the SoC steps (`slpa` and after) can close.

findings.title: A PMGR gate alone does not lose the storage controller
findings.body: genpd switched `ps_ans2` (the ANS, its mailbox and its SART) off in each of last night’s 4 suspends, and NVMe came back every time. So `slpa` takes away more than that gate does, perhaps the rail itself. The SART’s entries (8 of 16 used) are the first thing to check after the next `slpa` run.

findings.title: macOS writes the storage controller’s SART back on every start
findings.body: `IOSARTMapper::_setActive(true)` (13.5) copies the SART’s 16 config and 16 address words the first time, and writes them back every later time. The ANS start after sleep runs it. So macOS expects the SART to lose its entries in S2R, and the Linux SART driver had nothing for that. The test kernel now does the same.

findings: macOS tells the PMU the AP is asleep (`IOPMUBootStage` 0x50) in its sleep action, and gives the SMC a 10 s AP-watchdog deadline at the last quiesce step; Linux leaves 0x30 (“OS running”) through suspend, so a reset from sleep counts as a boot error

The PMGR’s AP wake-source mask (`0x29e00400c`, 1 = disabled) is 0 under Linux. macOS’s value, with only its 22 sources enabled, also stops the alarm and the EL2 timer from waking the boot CPU out of Aura’s deep WFI

The PMGR keeps per-state time counters (`AWAKE`, `SLP_S2R`, `SYS_S2R_AOP`, …), off under Linux. Turned on, they show the SoC stays AWAKE through Aura’s suspend and s2idle; in an `slpa` run that comes back they can prove a real S2R
PMGR counters after `slpa` plus the PMP steps (run C, 2026-11-05): `AWAKE` the whole 65 s, `SLP_S2R` 0. `slpa` does not put the SoC to sleep by itself; it only takes the storage controller down
The SART is intact after `slpa` (run C: `entries kept across suspend`); the ANS failure after `slpa` has another cause

The PMGR’s S2R timer (1 to MPMGR_AON + 0x4000, macOS’s `startS2RTimer`) resets the SoC about 60 s after it is written unless the S2R entry completes, whatever the alarm does (runs D, D2; 2026-11-05). With every core powered down macOS’s way it still resets (run E); the cores alone end in a WD1 reset (run F)

Apple coprocessors boot from an IO RVBAR in their ASC wrapper (`0x347050000` for the ANS, `0x28e850000` for the PMP), set and locked by iBoot; macOS rewrites it on every CPU start (`AppleASCWrapV4::_setIORVBAR`), Linux never does. It survives a normal suspend with `ps_ans2` gated and `slpa` too (run A, 2026-11-05 18:04), so it is not why the ANS fails after `slpa`

findings.title: The PMP crash was ours
findings.body: After `slpa` the PMP firmware crashed because the test kernel told it the AP’s sleep state twice; the firmware panics when given the state it already has. One request, as macOS sends, is the fix. The PMP still holds display and ISP requests that macOS releases before `slpa`.

findings.title: The storage controller does start after `slpa`
findings.body: Its firmware answers the first handshake but never acknowledges power-on, and its boot address and SART are intact. It most likely waits on the storage power the SMC cut, which a real S2R wake would restore. So the SoC sleep comes first.

findings.title: The PMP lets the displays go for sleep
findings.body: Withdrawing the three display requests in suspend and asserting them on resume works in a normal suspend; the PMP acks both. That puts the PMP close to macOS’s state at `slpa`; only ISP’s request differs.

findings.title: What we have now sleeps at 1.46 W
findings.body: An hour each on battery in one boot: suspend to RAM through Aura 1.458 W, s2idle 1.504 W, macOS 0.24 W. Parking the CPUs and releasing the display requests barely matter while the SoC stays up; the gap is the SoC sleep itself.

findings.title: macOS’s whole PMGR quiesce is not enough on its own
findings.body: With `slpa`, every core powered down and all of `quiesceHW` but the cluster power-off before the S2R timer, the SoC still resets 85 s later (runs G, H). The PMP now accepts its sleep request (run C). The next test does both in one sleep, as macOS does.

findings.title: Every macOS step found so far leaves the S2R entry incomplete
findings.body: `slpa`, the PMP's IDLE, the AOP's sleep handshake, the whole PMGR quiesce (clusters included) and every core powered down, all in one sleep (run J, 2026-11-06), still end in the S2R timer's reset at about 85 s. Not yet combined with them: macOS's PMGR wake mask (Linux enables every wake source; a pending one may hold the entry).

findings.title: The wake-mask step in suspend_late breaks the suspend by itself
findings.body: Writing the PMGR's AP wake mask from `suspend_late` ends in the 120 s dog even when the value is 0 (check run, 2026-11-06 15:44). So runs L and M (macOS's mask with `slpa` and the S2R timer) most likely stopped there, before `slpa`; they do not show that macOS's mask stops the timer or blocks every wake. The step now runs from the PM notifier.

findings.title: The PMGR wake mask needs a non-posted mapping; macOS's own mask keeps the alarm wake
findings.body: Every module access to the wake mask with a posted `ioremap()` stalled the SoC fabric (the DT's `/soc` is `nonposted-mmio`), so runs L and M and the 11-05 mask runs never tested a mask. With `ioremap_np()` the mask is written before the AOP's sleep message and restored on wake, and with macOS's 22 sources the PMU alarm still wakes Aura's deep WFI (2026-11-06 16:08). With the mask set, run L (every macOS step found so far) still ends in the S2R timer's reset at 86 s, so the mask is not what the entry waits for.

findings.title: The PMP's requests at 0 before slpa change nothing either
findings.body: Run N (2026-11-06 16:31) did L with the PMP's display and ISP requests released before `slpa`, so the PMP went IDLE with nothing requested, as in macOS: the S2R timer's reset at 86 s, as before. Next from macOS's trace: the PMGR stop request for each secondary core (image 55).

findings.title: Every step of macOS's sleep trace together still ends in the S2R timer's reset
findings.body: Run R (2026-11-06 16:41) did slpw, the PMP's requests at 0, slpa, the PMU boot stage, macOS's wake mask, the AOP handshake, the SMC's and PMP's IDLE, the whole quiesceHW with the clusters, the S2R timer, the secondaries' stop requests and every core in deep sleep, in macOS's order: reset at 86 s. What is left is the devices: Linux leaves PMGR power domains on that macOS has off by then.

findings.title: dwc3-apple oopses when a never-connected USB-C port is unbound
findings.body: Run U (2026-11-06 17:00): `dwc3_apple_remove()` takes its lock through `platform_get_drvdata()`, which only `dwc3_core_probe()` sets on the first cable event, so unbinding a port with no cable since boot dereferences NULL (+0x5b0). The unbind runs now skip ports without an xHCI. Ports with a cable are syscore devices by design, so their `atc*_usb` domain stays on in every suspend.

findings.title: Unbinding a device keeps its PM domains on (DEFER_OFF)
findings.body: Run U2 (2026-11-06 17:11) unbound the display stack and a USB-C port and came back on the alarm, but only the PMP's display domains went off (96 of 200 still on). The PMGR driver gives every domain that is on at boot GENPD_FLAG_DEFER_OFF, so genpd keeps a domain on while any DT consumer has no bound driver, and ACTIVE_WAKEUP keeps it on for a device on a wakeup path. The next step is a per-domain dump of why each one is held.

findings.title: Why Linux keeps 19 PM domains on at sleep
findings.body: Run S3 (2026-11-06 17:18) printed genpd's reason per domain: the three DCPs put themselves on a wake path in suspend (the driver says it cannot fully shut the DCP down yet), which holds 13 display domains including afr; the USB-C controllers are syscore while their core is up, or have wakeup enabled (3 domains); sio and the apcie_gp pair stay on for DT always-on children. Whether the PMGR's S2R entry waits for them is the next test.

findings.title: Turning the held display and USB-C domains off in Aura hangs a normal suspend
findings.body: Run Y (2026-11-06 17:31): with Aura switching the 12 domains Linux keeps on (the three display chains, the three USB-C ports) off before its wait and back on after, the normal-path suspend ended in the 120 s watchdog; without that step it comes back. Either the writes stall the fabric or Linux's resume hangs on devices that lost their state. Image 57 lets each group be tested alone (runs Y1 to Y3).

findings.title: Turning the USB-C domains off from Aura stalls the SoC; the S2R timer works without slpa
findings.body: Runs Y1T and T0 (2026-11-06 17:48 and 17:54): the S2R timer alone resets the SoC about 85 s after echo mem on a normal suspend, but written after the USB-C domain-off step it never fires (145 s, the watchdog). Aura stalls in that step, most likely because the USB controllers keep running through the suspend (syscore xHCI) and losing their power wedges the fabric. They must be stopped by Linux first.

findings.title: Aura cannot force the held domains off; Linux must quiesce them first
findings.body: Run Y2T (2026-11-06 17:59): the external displays' domains (nothing attached) off from Aura, then the S2R timer: WD1 at 145 s, as Y1T for USB-C. Aura stalls in the domain-off step whenever the domain's devices are still running (DCP firmware, syscore xHCI). The held domains must be powered off by genpd after their drivers stop the devices (USB-C wake paths and xHCI; DCP RTKit shutdown and cold start), then the S2R entry is tried with them off.

findings.title: With wakeup off, genpd powers an idle USB-C port's domain off; live ports are held as syscore
findings.body: Run S4 (2026-11-06 18:08): disabling power/wakeup on the dwc3-apple devices let genpd turn atc1_usb (no cable) off in noirq and on again at resume (98 of 200 domains on, S3 99; back on the alarm in 32.8 s). atc0_usb (charger, device mode) and atc2_usb (xHCI with a receiver) stay on because dwc3-apple marks a port with its core up as syscore. Next: tear such ports down before a deep suspend and bring them up after it.

findings.title: A deep-suspend teardown in dwc3-apple frees every USB-C domain; USB comes back
findings.body: Run S5 (2026-11-06 18:17): with dwc3_apple.test_deep_teardown (stop a live core at PM_SUSPEND_PREPARE as a cable removal would, restart it in its role at PM_POST_SUSPEND) and phy_apple_atc.test_restore_pd_off (the T8103-table PHY restores itself after its domain was off), atc0_usb and atc2_usb go off in sleep: 96 of 200 domains on (S3 99). Back on the alarm in 32.7 s; the receiver re-enumerated and the charger port is in device mode again. Left: the three DCP chains (13 domains, wake path by design) and two always-on groups.

findings.title: With the DCP firmware shut down, genpd turns every device-held domain off: 83 of 200 on
findings.body: Run S6 (2026-11-06 21:19): appledrm.test_sleep_off shuts each DCP's RTKit firmware down in suspend instead of claiming the wake path; with the USB-C teardown all 13 display domains and 3 USB-C domains go off in noirq. At syscore suspend 83 of 200 domains are on (S3 99): the DT's always-on ones plus sio and the apcie_gp pair, held by always-on children. Back on the alarm in 32.8 s; the DCPs stay dead (not restarted yet) and the GPU's gfx domain failed to power on at resume (new).

findings.title: With every device-held domain off, the S2R entry still ends in the timer's reset
findings.body: Run R6 (2026-11-06 21:26): run R's full macOS sleep sequence (slpa, SetAPPower, quiesceHW, the S2R timer, CPU stop requests, deep sleep) plus S6's Linux-side domain-offs (83 of 200 on): the next kernel came 86.0 s after echo mem, the timer's reset, as in R. The devices' power domains are not what the PMGR's S2R entry waits for. Left from the macOS trace: the PMP's CPU-complex requests (PCPM0/1), which macOS clears after slpa and Linux never asserts.

findings.title: The PMP acknowledges CPU-complex (PCPM0/1) requests from Linux
findings.body: Run S7 (2026-11-06 21:36): pmp_report.test_pcpm 0x300 asserted at PM_SUSPEND_PREPARE (request and ack 0xf300) and withdrawn after the wake (0xf000), each acknowledged; a normal suspend came back as before. Run R7 (the same withdrawn after slpa and the PMP's IDLE, as macOS's trace step 6) waits for an attended first run.

findings.title: The GPU domain hangs off afr, which went off for the first time in S6
findings.body: gfx has parents gpx (always-on) and afr; afr's other child is dispext0_sys. With the display chain off (S6), afr powered off, and at resume gfx did not reach its on state (BUSY, actual 0). afr may need state restored after a power-off, or gfx the PMP's GFX request.

findings.title: afr going off breaks the GPU's power-up after sleep
findings.body: Run S8 (2026-11-06 21:41): S6 with pmgr_pwrstate.test_sleep_keep=afr (84 of 200 on): the GPU's gfx domain powered up after the wake without error, unlike S6. afr, gfx's parent, comes back from a power-off without what gfx needs. Test runs keep afr on; a real S2R needs the GPU bring-up to cope with afr having lost power.

findings.title: AMCC errors DSID_AGE_OUT and UNEXP_RT_HIT_DIR are enabled and pending before the commit
findings.body: Run G58 (2026-11-06 22:30, image 58 records): every one of the 4 AMCC instances has error status word 0 bit 26 (DSID_AGE_OUT) and word 1 bit 8 (UNEXP_RT_HIT_DIR) set, both enabled (plane 0 enables 0xb7bffdfd / 0x3f00), on the normal path just before Aura's wait. On T8140 (DJ) exactly this wakes the SoC within 20 ms of the S2R commit when no platform error handler runs; macOS clears the enables at quiesce. R8 clears them (aura-ctl 0x200).

findings.title: WD2 sits at a 90 s alarm, disabled, counter running
findings.body: Run G58: WD2 (WDT + 0x20) alarm 0x80befc00 = 90 s, ctl 0, counter running (about 87 s at entry); iBoot's leftover, as on the M1 (Naeem, try28). WD1 is Aura's 120 s suspend dog. Whether the S2R timer's reset about 60 s after its write is WD2 is run W1's question.

findings.title: WD2 is involved in the reset after the S2R timer, but is not the only one
findings.body: Run W1 (2026-11-06 22:34): the S2R timer with WD2 stopped 100 ms later reset about 116 s after echo mem, not 85 s (T0) or 145 s (WD1). The 30 s alarm did not resume Linux. Next: image 59 resumes the kernel right after the timer so Linux can log the watchdogs until the reset.

findings.title: Clearing the AMCC error enables and masking the AIC does not complete the entry
findings.body: Run R8 (2026-11-06 22:41, owner attended): R7 (every macOS step found, slpa, PCPM0/1, devices off, afr kept) plus the AMCC DSID_AGE_OUT/UNEXP_RT_HIT_DIR enables cleared before the S2R timer and every AIC line masked after it: the timer's reset at 86 s again. Next: the CPU-complex power gates and CLLT writes that the t8103 and T8140 entries have and Aura does not.

findings.title: After the S2R timer is written, Linux cannot be resumed
findings.body: Run W2 (2026-11-06 23:01, image 59, aura-ctl 0x2101): the S2R timer, then Aura returned straight to the kernel (the same psci_resume_kernel as a normal wake, without the wait). Linux printed nothing more, its network never came back, and the next kernel started 86 s after echo mem, the timer's usual reset. W1 showed Aura's own code still runs at least 100 ms after the timer, so the CPU and DRAM keep working, but the kernel's resume does not get through. The timer write is the point of no return; the watchdogs after it cannot be logged from Linux.

findings.title: Aura's armed WD1 does not keep the S2R entry from completing
findings.body: Run R9 (2026-11-06 23:08, owner attended): R8 (every macOS step found, slpa, PCPM0/1, devices off, afr kept, AMCC errors cleared, AIC masked) plus WD1 disarmed right before the S2R timer, so every AON watchdog but WD2 is off at the commit as in macOS: the next kernel 86 s after echo mem, the timer's reset again.

findings.title: The PMU marks the AP asleep at the timer reset
findings.body: boot-error-stage (PMU 0x6003) reads 0x50 after the timer resets of every run that sent macOS's slpa and SetAPPower 0x201 (I, J, L, N, R, R6, R8, R9) and 0x30 after every other kind of boot. Linux never writes it, so the SMC/PMU firmware sets it on the AP-sleep messages: the SMC side considers the AP asleep, and the missing part is on the SoC side.

findings.title: The PMU has free scratch that Aura can write
findings.body: 13.5's AppleDialogSPMIPMU uses legacy scratch keys 0-3, 8-11, 0xf, 0x18-0x1a and 0x1f (base 0x6000). Keys 4-7, 0xc-0xe, 0x10-0x17 and 0x1b-0x1e are unused; 0x6004 takes a write from Linux and reads it back. Image 60 puts Aura's stage codes there.

findings.title: The boot core gets through Aura's whole sleep tail
findings.body: Run R10 (image 60b, 2026-11-06 23:43): PMU scratch 0x6004 = 0x18 after the 86 s timer reset. Aura wrote the timer, stopped WD2, masked the AIC and released the secondaries, and reached the point before its cache flush and deep WFI. It never returned from the WFI and never came back through RVBAR.

findings.title: Naeem Malik's M1 sleeps once the last core reaches its WFI
findings.body: malik-na/m1-power-lab (11-06/07): his ~5 s post-commit resets came from his own last core hanging on an MMIO access to a clock-parked USB controller. With no hardware access after the commit (try32) the M1 really slept, woke on the RTC alarm at the locked RVBAR, and held 0.05 W over 3 hours (try46).

findings.title: At the last moment one P complex is still on
findings.body: Run R11 (image 60c, 2026-11-07 06:29): the boot core reached its deep WFI (code 0x19) and the PMP's requests were all released (0), but 2 ms after the secondaries' release the PCPM0 power word was still on while PCPM1 was off. Aura's park loop never acks the release IPI (IPI_SR), so released secondaries may spin instead of powering down.

findings.title: With IPI_SR cleared both P complexes power down; E core 3 does not sleep
findings.body: Run R12 (image 60d, 2026-11-07 06:36): the boot core reached its deep WFI again, PCPM0 and PCPM1 both read actual state 0 and PACC0/1 bit 4 cleared, so the release-IPI ack fixed R11's lit P complex. Every P core and E cores 1-2 reached the S2R sleep; E core 3 (MPIDR 3) never did. The timer still reset the Mac at 86 s.

findings.title: cpu3 gets the release IPI but never leaves its park WFI
findings.body: Run R13 (image 60e, 2026-11-07 06:48): Aura held cpus 1-6 and 8-10 as CPU_OFF and sent each the release IPI; all but cpu3 reached the S2R sleep. cpu3 was CPU_OFF too. Both P complexes were off within 6 ms. The timer still reset the Mac at 86 s.

findings.title: Nothing wakes cpu3 from its park WFI at the release
findings.body: Run R14 (image 60f, 2026-11-07 06:55): cpu3 was sent the release IPI at its own MPIDR, had entered its park loop once, and never came out of that WFI, not even for a second IPI 2 ms later. cpus 1 and 2 on the same path wake. Suspects, all done to the E cluster before the release: the CPUSTART stop request (aura-ctl bit 5), the cluster targets and the clock parking.

findings.title: Without the CPUSTART stop request every core reaches its final deep sleep
findings.body: Run R15 (image 60f, aura-ctl 0x5b1f, 2026-11-07 07:02): without Aura's per-core CPUSTART+0 stop request before the release IPI, cpu3 slept too. All 9 secondaries were in cpu_sleep(true), the boot core reached its deep WFI and both P complexes were off. The SoC still did not sleep: timer reset at 86 s. Next: no hardware access after the commit (image 60g).

findings.title: Naeem's quiet commit alone does not finish the entry; Aura never turned off the boot cluster
findings.body: Run R16 (image 60g, aura-ctl 0xdb1f, 2026-11-07 07:09): every hardware access before the S2R timer, the timer written three times, nothing after it but the flush and deep WFI; every core slept, both P complexes off; still the 86 s reset. Static: 13.5's AppleT6020PMGR::quiesceHW turns off logical clusters from 1, and the ADT soc-clusters byte 3 makes cluster 1 EACC (the boot cluster), 2 PACC0, 3 PACC1. Image 54 used byte 0 and never wrote EACC; R16's snapshot shows EACC target 0xf. The M1 entry also writes both CPU complexes off before the commit. Image 60h adds it (R17).

findings.title: With EACC off too the entry still does not finish; the SEP is never told to sleep
findings.body: Run R17 (image 60h, aura-ctl 0x1db1f, 2026-11-07 07:22): EACC's target reached 0, all else as R16; still the 86 s reset. The CPU-complex PS words read target 0 even awake. 13.5's AppleSEPManager::_sleepSEPAsync sends the SEP a SLEEP control message (EP 0, opcode 0x0c, type 2) before system sleep; Linux's apple-sep never does. Testing it touches SEP state shared with macOS, so it waits for the owner.

findings.title: The SEP's SLEEP message decoded; test R18 built, not armed
findings.body: cmsgSLEEP's 8-byte message is 0x000c0000 with the sleep type in byte 3 (EP 0, op 0x0c, param 2, data 0); its u32 argument is the reply timeout (15 s outside simulators), not data. The J414s SEP node has a single always-on domain (ps_sep), so the driver holds nothing extra. apple_sep.test_sleep_msg (default 0) sends it at PM_SUSPEND_PREPARE; run R18 = R17 + type 2. The module is not installed until the owner answers.

findings.title: SIO, MTP and the SEP run into every commit awake; macOS sleeps every IOP through RTBuddy
findings.body: macOS's trace covered only the SMC and the PMP. In macOS, RTBuddy::setPowerState puts every RTKit coprocessor to sleep at system sleep. At our commit Linux has told the SMC, PMP and AOP (0x201) and shut the DCPs down, but the SEP, SIO (sio_suspend is a TODO stub) and MTP (rtkit-helper, built in, no PM ops) get nothing. apple_sio.test_sleep_idle (default off) sends RTKit IDLE 0x201 in .suspend; run R19 = R17 + that.

findings.title: SIO IDLE before the commit: still the 86 s reset (R19)
findings.body: Run R19 (image 60h, aura-ctl 0x1db1f, apple_sio.test_sleep_idle=Y, 2026-11-07 07:43): echo mem to the next kernel 85 s, PMU scratch identical to R17 (code 0x16). The SIO's ack is not visible: the kmsg stream stops before the device .suspend phase and the journal is lost. A normal-path run (S9) is to confirm the SIO accepts IDLE.

findings.title: The SIO acks RTKit IDLE; it is not what the entry waits for (S9)
findings.body: Run S9 (normal path, 2026-11-07 07:51): apple-sio 'TEST: firmware IDLE for system sleep: 0', back on the alarm in 32.4 s with all CPUs. With R19 (same step before the commit, still 86 s) the SIO is ruled out. Left: the SEP (R18, waits for the owner), MTP (built into the kernel), the GPU.

findings.title: maralcbr's post-slpa writes: most are already in Aura; the cluster APSC disable is new
findings.body: A static second pass (2026-11-07) over the trace's 74 writes. Aura's CLOCKS (ClkGen-SOC, T6000 offsets +4), PLL-off (0x28e224000, same sequence), CLUSTERS/EACC (soc-cluster words, T6000 at +0x10000) and DOMAINS (ps_sio_cpu AUTO_ENABLE) steps match the trace entry for entry, independently of our macOS 13.5 J414s RE. The PCIe write is in config space on T6020, the four die-quadrant error-handler writes fall outside every J414s reg, and the pmgr_dcp/PMP-report pre-slpa words sit in a window whose layout differs between chips: none are replayed. The J414s ADT turns APSC on (cpu-apsc = 1) and leaves the ppt/llc/amx throttles off, so the trace's one new cluster write is APSC_DIS (bit 23 on T6020, bit 22 on T6000). Image 61 adds it (run R20).

findings.title: Cluster APSC off before the release IPIs hangs the SoC; the S2R timer does not reset (R20)
findings.body: Run R20 (image 61, aura-ctl 0x3db1f, 2026-11-07 08:28): code 0x16 reached, but only Aura cpus 4 and 8 reached their S2R sleep (never-slept feee; cpu1 CPU_OFF, park-loop WFI never returned, a second IPI did not wake it), PCPM0 stayed on (0x6014 ff), and for the first time the timer did not reset the SoC: it hung until the owner held power 28 min later. R13 had an awake core and still reset at 86 s, so the APSC disable itself seems to block the timer's reset. macOS disables APSC only after its secondaries sleep; a variant after the snapshot (R20b) is possible but owner-present only. R18 (SEP SLEEP) runs first.

findings.title: The SEP SLEEP message is acknowledged but not what the entry waits for (R18)
findings.body: Run R18 (2026-11-07 09:27, R17 + apple_sep.test_sleep_msg=2): the enclave replied (tag 0x11, data 0), and the run ended in the same 86 s timer reset with PMU scratch identical to R17's. macOS 15.6.1 then clears the SEP mailbox OUTBOX_CTRL enable and writes 0x1000030f to the SEP's PMGR word (PS_AUTO 0, so the PMGR may gate the enclave); J414s ps_sep reads 0x1f0000ff (PS_AUTO f, never gated). R18B adds that step; built, waits for the owner to be present.

findings.title: Three fabric lanes (and the SEP) are never allowed to auto-gate on J414s; macOS sets their floor to 0
findings.body: From maralcbr's T6000 sleep-entry PMGR dump mapped by DT label: AFNC1_LW2, AFNC2_LW1, APCIE_GP_SYS and SEP read 0x1f0000ff on J414s (AUTO_ENABLE, PS_AUTO f), macOS has 0x1000030f (PS_AUTO 0) at sleep entry; AFNC3_LW0 already matches. Linux's pmgr-pwrstate never writes PS_AUTO. Image 62 (run R21) and R18B test it.

findings.title: Every sleep step found so far, in one sleep, still ends in the 86 s reset
findings.body: The runs of 2026-11-05 to 07: `slpa`, the PMP and AOP handshakes, the SIO IDLE, the whole PMGR quiesce, the held domains off, the AMCC clear, every core and both P complexes powered down, a quiet commit. The PMU scratch after the reset is byte for byte the same from R17 to R19. The S2R entry still waits for something not yet found.

findings.title: The SEP probe flake was a loader race
findings.body: Two units loaded `apple_sep`, and `aurora-sep-load` unloaded the packaged load mid-attach, so the second probe hit the one-shot marker (`-EBUSY`, key type registered then unregistered 2 ms later). Fixed on 2026-11-08: the script now only loads when the module is absent. It had cost R18B its first try.

findings.title: Limine’s one-shot entry survives a reboot under U-Boot
findings.body: `bootctl set-oneshot DeepTest` (the Boot Loader Interface’s `LoaderEntryOneShot`) booted the test entry once and the next boot was the default again (2026-11-09, 1 of 1). That replaces GRUB’s `next_entry` on the new Limine install.

findings.title: A test `boot.bin` can be made one-shot with a PMU scratch byte
findings.body: PMU legacy scratch key 0x10 (0x6010) survives a reset and is writable from the stock kernel through nvmem. A stage 2 built from the stock source with one patch reads it: 0xa5 means clear it, start the watchdog and chainload `m1n1/boot-test.bin`; anything else is a normal boot. So a hung test chain costs one watchdog reset, not a trip to recoveryOS. First boot of the loader is still to do (2026-11-10).

findings.title: The PMU alarm fired only once per boot because of a latch bit
findings.body: On T602x the PMU sets bit 1 of the alarm control byte (0x1401) when an alarm fires. While it is set, later alarms raise no event and no interrupt. Our first port kept the bit. Clearing it on every control write fixed it (run K5c). aurora-silicon found the same independently on 2026-11-09 (`0dd76c9db67a`).

findings.title: aurora-silicon’s M4 Pro S2R points at domains we leave on
findings.body: Their T6040 controller (linux PR 1477, three complete resumes) follows macOS’s rule that every “axi2af” fabric-bridge domain must be off at the commit: the USB-C commons, the display systems, ANS, the video blocks, PCIe. With some on, their S2R timer reset the SoC instead of sleeping, which is our symptom. Our run S8 dump shows `atc0-3_common`, `atc0-3_pcie` and `apcie_gp_sys` on at every commit; macOS has them off. Image 63 lowers the USB-C ones. T8140’s longer sequence (DCS ladder, MCC stop, PMC voters) is not used on T6040, so it is not a candidate for T6020.

findings.title: The secure enclave can be put in macOS’s sleep state, and it is not the blocker
findings.body: After its SLEEP message the enclave holds its own power floor up until the host shuts the mailbox’s outbox; then it drops the floor within 200 ms and is power-gated, and its mailbox no longer answers (reading it hangs the reader). Aura now does this at the start of its quiesce. With it every word of macOS’s sleep-entry power map matches, and the SoC still resets on the S2R timer (run R18K, 2026-11-10).

findings.title: The domains macOS has off at sleep entry are not what blocks the power-down
findings.body: Runs R17A to R17D (2026-11-10) set every power word that macOS has off at sleep entry and ours left on to target 0 before the commit: the eight USB-C words, the PCIe chain, `atc1-3_usb_aon`, `msg`, `pmp` and `pms_sram`. A crumb in the PMU scratch showed each one off at the last access before the commit. All four runs ended in the timer’s reset about 86 s later, as before. Only the SEP’s word still differs.

findings.title: macOS’s own T6020 kernel and device tree can be read on this Mac
findings.body: A read-only APFS reader opens macOS’s unencrypted Preboot volume from Linux. Its 15.7.1 kernelcache and the J414s device tree show that the PMU driver, not the PMGR, fires the S2R timer, after scheduling the wake alarm; that the M4 Pro’s keep-alive step has no T6020 counterpart; and that the secure enclave sets its own power-gating floor, idling at macOS’s sleep-entry value.

findings.title: The reset after the commit is the S2R timer, not a wake that failed
findings.body: Run R22B (2026-11-11) repeated the commit with the wake alarm at +70 s instead of +40 s. Main’s kernel started 76 s after the commit either way, before a boot from the later alarm could have got there. So the SoC is not asleep when the alarm is due; the entry itself does not finish. This had last been checked on 2026-11-05, before any of macOS’s entry steps were in place.

findings.title: No debug power request holds the cores up
findings.body: macOS’s kernel unlocks each core’s external debug block and writes EDPRCR := 0 before the core’s last WFI, so a debugger cannot keep it powered. Image 72 does the same on all 10 cores (run R21). The register already read 0 on every core, and the reset came as before.

findings.title: After the commit one P cluster is really off; the other and the E cluster still answer
findings.body: Run R23 (2026-11-11) kept one P core awake for 3 s after the boot core’s last instruction. It saw the boot cluster’s power word change within 16 ms and stay, and the PMU and PMGR still answering. That was first read as “every cluster is off, the block is above the cores”. Runs R24A and R24B corrected it: the second P cluster’s word reads off even with a core running in it, so the words are not proof. What does differ is the debug blocks: a sleeping core’s block in the first P cluster does not answer (power really gone), while the second P cluster’s and the E cluster’s do. The likely reading is that those cores sit in their last wait-for-interrupt loop without losing power.

findings.title: The sleep engine reacts to the commit in under 4 ms, then parks
findings.body: The commit (three writes of 1 to the S2R timer word) changes exactly five words of the always-on PMGR block, all within 4 ms (runs R35B–E, control R35C unchanged, trace R36A), moves the PMGR system state to SYS_SLP_DDR and reloads WD2 to 60 s. Then nothing: the SoC-level state stays AWAKE until WD2 resets the Mac 61 s later. macOS never writes those words itself, so they are the engine’s status. What it waits for is not another step in this block. Open: whether the sleeping cores, the SMC/PMP handshake or an unreadable part of the block (pages 8–10 hang the reader) is the missing condition, and whether the awake observer core is itself holding AWAKE.

findings.title: macOS writes the S2R timer twice and touches nothing else in the always-on block
findings.body: A macOSTest run under the hypervisor (2026-11-12) traced every guest access to MPMGR_AON pages 0 to 7 and to the AP wake block. Through boot and a full sleep entry the only access was two writes of 1 to the S2R timer by CPU 0, after the PCPM and USB hooks and after the CPU stop requests, with the cores going into deep sleep after it. macOS never reads or writes the five words the commit changes, so they are the engine’s own status. Our commit writes the timer three times and does not send the CPU stop requests before it; both are being tried.

findings.title: Our PMGR state at the commit differs from macOS’s in 59 words, none of them the cause
findings.body: A macOSTest run read macOS’s own PMGR power words at its S2R timer write; Aura compared our 374 readable ones right before our commit: 59 differ in desired or actual state (the cores, a few fabric words, PCIe, SIO, PWM, I2C, SPI, SPMI, UARTs, audio, DPA). Forcing all 50 non-core ones to macOS’s state before the commit, together with every other step the hypervisor shows, left the result unchanged. The engine’s five words are at macOS’s resting values at its commit, and no wake source stands. What remains is outside what the hypervisor and our observers can see.

findings.title: macOS's own deep sleep, run under our hypervisor, also resets about 60 s later
findings.body: With a rebuilt hypervisor that lets macOS's real sleep writes (all ten cores' ACC_OVRD and CYC_OVRD) reach the hardware, macOS 14.8.9 on the J414s did not wake at its 5-minute alarm: the Mac dropped off USB exactly 60 s after the cores' last sleep write and rebooted, the same shape as every Linux run. So either something in the test setup (the hypervisor, or the guest's boot-args with PCIe and CLPC off) blocks the sleep, or macOS needs something we don't know about either. Stock macOS's baseline wake is still unmeasured.

findings.title: A stock-macOS sleep baseline needs macOSTest’s own boot object, not m1n1
findings.body: 2026-11-14 09:05: macOSTest armed one-shot for a native boot (no Pi, no hypervisor). macOSTest’s boot object is m1n1, so it does not start macOS by itself; the one-shot was used up and the Mac came back to Omarchy with no result. A native baseline needs macOSTest’s boot object switched back to the stock kernel (recoveryOS, kmutil configure-boot) and m1n1 put back afterwards for hypervisor runs. Not done.

findings.title: macOS writes an SMC key, pmVC, between slpw and slpa; our test kernel never has
findings.body: 2026-11-15: comparing our entry with the merged M5 Pro (T6050) sleep driver found its SMC lane writes pmVC (a ui32 policy key) with fixed spacings between slpw and slpa, and its binding says there is no deep sleep without them. macOS on this M2 Pro does the same: every hypervisor log (latew, unmask, realsleep) shows MBSE=slpw, then pmVC = bytes 01 01 00 00, then WKTP = 2, then MBSE=slpa. Our TEST macsmc-reboot deep_steps sends slpw, WKTP and slpa and never pmVC. Not yet tested.

findings.title: Run R48A: adding pmVC and WKTP to the SMC handshake changed nothing
findings.body: 2026-11-15 16:59 (image 98, deep_steps 191 = 62 + WKTP + pmVC after slpw, root with the new macsmc-reboot module): committed 16:59:29, the usual reset, back on main about 80 s later, last crumb stage 0x16 as in every commit run. No wake, no timing change. Not captured: the kernel line that says whether the pmVC write returned 0 (the job log has no dmesg of it), so the SMC accepting the key is assumed from deep_steps=191 taking effect, not shown.

findings.title: Overnight s2idle with the PMP on: resumes, but 1.75 W
findings.body: 2026-11-15 20:58 to 2026-11-16 15:04 (daily boot: Aura PR 268, PR 933 DTB, kernel 7.2.11-15-1-ARCH): 18.1 h in s2idle, resumed on a key, 31.6 Wh used (1.75 W average). The AOP mailbox woke the SoC 3.6 times a second all night (99.9% of 54,494 wakes) and 19 power domains stayed on. No run without the PMP yet, so the PMP is not shown to be the cause.

findings.title: Asked DJ: the 60 s is WD2, armed by the commit; M1 Pro deep sleep exists (Andreas Fernandez)
findings.body: 2026-11-16: DJ (T8140 deep sleep) asked whether the reset is a fixed watchdog or the S2R timer. Our R34 measurement: the commit reloads WD2 to 60 s (T8140 uses 5 s) and moves the PMGR to SYS_SLP_DDR while the SoC stays awake; moving the alarm to +20/+40/+70 s or the watchdog to 120/200 s changes nothing. He pointed us to a working M1 Pro (T6000, J314s) deep sleep by Andreas Fernandez (GitHub Ante042, branch t600x-s2r-reference of his linux and m1n1 forks): hundreds of sleeps on his machine, about 150 mW overnight. It is not for our T6020, but it is the reference to compare our sequence with; anything reused keeps his authorship. Our #933 (J414s PMP) merged the same day.

findings.title: Compared with the M1 Pro deep sleep: our sequence matches it step for step
findings.body: 2026-11-16: image 98 against Andreas Fernandez's t6000 driver (his branch t600x-s2r-reference): same core power-down overrides, L1 flush, core stops before the S2R timer and the timer last, same SMC/PMP/AOP/SEP steps (SEP read idle live), WD0 already off. The SEP, per-core deep-WFI and watchdog candidates are closed. The difference left is the chip: his is T6000, ours T6020.

findings.title: The SMC accepts pmVC and WKTP (return code 0)
findings.body: 2026-11-16 run R49A: slpw, pmVC = 0x101 and WKTP = 2 each return 0 on the M2 Pro, so the SMC handshake is not what keeps the sleep from completing. The commit itself did not run in that job (the display driver refused a second suspend after my extra test pass).

findings.title: Two more differences from the M1 Pro deep sleep tried: no change
findings.body: 2026-11-16 run R50A (Aura image 99): one S2R timer write instead of two, and the deep sleep path stopping the core timers and setting IRQ/FIQ mode 2 on every core, as Andreas Fernandez's t6000 driver does. The SoC still resets about 80 s after the commit. Still untested: his thin stage 1 (needs the main install's stage 1 replaced).

findings.title: s2idle without the PMP drains 2.0 W, with it 1.75 W: one night each
findings.body: 2026-11-16/17: the same boot chain (Aura PR 268) with the PMP off (stock J414s device tree) drained 2.003 W over 9.19 h suspended (40.49 to 22.06 Wh, 3.85 AOP wakes per second per CPU, 16 domains left on). The PMP night before drained 1.746 W over 18.11 h (3.6 wakes per second, 19 domains on). So the PMP saves about 0.26 W in s2idle on these two nights, and does not change the AOP wake rate. Caveats: one night each, different lengths, and this one ran on the charger with the battery force-discharged while the earlier one was on battery (the first hour of a suspend drains more: the first 49 minutes here read 2.52 W). The October note that the PMP does not change s2idle drain (1.4 W) is from a different kernel and setup.

findings.title: R52B: the SIO axi2af tunables (decoded from macOS) did not change the commit
findings.body: 2026-11-17: all 22 tunables of the T6020 _af_sioaxi2af_figs_1 table (bridge at 0x39a000000, reg = (reg & ~clear) | set; none were applied under Linux) were written and read back before the SEP sleep, then the usual R50A commit. SEP asleep, commit taken, no wake: the SoC reset about 86 s later as before. The SMC AP deadline (0x29e2a002c) reads 0 here, so zeroing it is a no-op; our PCIe step already reads the GP domains at actual state 0. Everything in the Nov 17 comment on issue 5 that applies to a native Aura entry is now matched or shown moot; what is left is the thin stage 1 and their hypervisor-side cluster handling.

findings.title: R54A: nekolyanich's commit order (commit 1, AIC mask-all, 0.52 ms, commit 2) did not change the reset; code audit found a secondary-stop race in LATEREL
findings.body: 2026-11-18 (image 100, fifth aura-ctl word 63): all 22 SIO axi2af tunables applied, SEP asleep, commit reached (crumb 0x16, 45 PMGR words forced), no wake — main kernel started 77 s after the commit push (86 s to userspace return, matching ~6 s suspend + ~60 s WD2 + boot time). Auditing psci.c/smp.c after R54A exposed a bug affecting R40A through R54A: smp_psci_stop_parked() wrote CPUSTART+0 and waited 40 ms while secondaries were already sitting in retention WFI_MODE(3), powering both P complexes off before the commit so post-commit release IPIs hit already-stopped cores; and cpu_sleep_setup(true) wrote cluster-wide ACC_OVRD on every core instead of only the last core per cluster. Image 101 fixes both by holding all 9 secondaries awake in WFE until cpu0's edge.

findings.title: R55A: edge-hold WFE confirmed all 9 secondaries awake through CPUSTART+0, and exposed psci_force_ps() turning PCIe/USB/ANS/SIO domains back ON since R45A
findings.body: 2026-11-18 (image 101, fifth aura-ctl word 127): PMU scratch confirmed all 9 secondaries (0x077e) held awake in WFE before quiesce and after CPUSTART+0 with ECPM/PCPM0 on (1f/1f) and PMP+SEP off (0x50), still resetting at +77 s to kernel.
